=== NOTES 2:113 | Processes of Social Change – Sanskritisation, Westernisation, Modernisation, Secularisation
## SUB 0 | Culture Contact – Acculturation, Assimilation, Pluralism, Ethnocentrism
[113:0:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [113:0:0.0] Acculturation | Change through sustained contact: a group is influenced by another (dominant) culture and its way of life changes, but it stays distinct
  [113:0:0.1] Assimilation ("merger") | A group (e.g. immigrants) loses its own cultural identity and is absorbed into the host/dominant culture
  [113:0:0.2] Integration | Taking part in the wider society while retaining identity
  [113:0:0.3] Amalgamation | Biological/cultural fusion of groups into a new one ("melting pot")
  [113:0:0.4] Cultural pluralism / multiculturalism | Peaceful coexistence of distinct groups and cultures in one society
  [113:0:0.5] Cultural diffusion | Spread of culture (e.g. through media)
  [113:0:0.6] Cultural relativism | Understanding a culture on its own terms
  [113:0:0.7] Ethnocentrism | Own group seen as the centre of everything and superior; others rated by it (Sumner)
  [113:0:0.8] Xenocentrism / Xenophobia | Preferring other cultures / fear of foreigners
  [113:0:0.9] Ethnic group | Group sharing a common culture
  [113:0:0.10] Regionalism / Communalism / Casteism | Loyalty to a region / religious group / caste
[113:0:1] - **⚠ Trap:** pluralism = coexistence; amalgamation = fusion; assimilation = identity lost; acculturation = influenced but distinct.
[113:0:2] - **Ghurye**, *The Aborigines So-Called and Their Future*: argued for **tribal assimilation** (tribes as "backward Hindus").
[113:0:3] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Society p.19-20; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Society Part 2 p.36-37; app notes 2:113 sub 2
## SUB 1 | Sanskritisation and Dominant Caste (M.N. Srinivas)
[113:1:0] - **Coined by M.N. Srinivas** in *Religion and Society among the Coorgs of South India* (**1952**); developed in *Social Change in Modern India*; first called **"Brahminisation"**.
[113:1:1] - **Meaning:** a **low caste, tribe or group** adopts the customs, rituals and way of life of a higher, **twice-born** caste (**imitates the upper-caste lifestyle**, observes its rites) to claim a higher rank.
[113:1:2] - **Reference groups:** Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas or the **local dominant caste**.
[113:1:3] - A claim to higher status succeeds only when the caste wins **acceptance by others** (group recognition), usually after economic or political gains.
[113:1:4] - Brings **positional, not structural** change – **upward mobility** for a caste, hierarchy intact; **downward mobility** is no part of it.
[113:1:5] - **De-sanskritisation:** rejecting Sanskritic norms and asserting own identity (non-Brahmin / Dravidian movements).
[113:1:6] - **Dominant caste** (Srinivas): concept also his; used to study **stratification in rural India**.
[113:1:7] - Srinivas's set: **Sanskritisation + Westernisation + Secularisation + Dominant Caste**.
[113:1:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Society p.5, p.13, p.18; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Society Part 3 p.13-14; app notes 2:113 sub 3
## SUB 2 | Social Change – Meaning, Sources and Theories
[113:2:0] # Meaning and sources
[113:2:1] - **Social change** = **alteration in the social order** (structure and relationships) of a society.
[113:2:2] TABLE head: Factor | Example
  [113:2:2.0] Technology | Industrial Revolution (Watt, Hargreaves; term popularised in English by Arnold Toynbee, 1760-1820); internet – 820 million+ users (Dec 2025)
  [113:2:2.1] Education | Spread of modern education
  [113:2:2.2] Law | Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955; widow remarriage and sati laws
  [113:2:2.3] Media | Spreads awareness, forms opinion; cultural diffusion; behaviour-change communication (ES 2025-26)
  [113:2:2.4] Migration / urbanisation | Industrialisation and urbanisation
  [113:2:2.5] Planning | Green Revolution; inclusive growth (11th Plan)
[113:2:3] - **Seasonal migration of nomads** is a routine cycle – **NOT** a source of social change.
[113:2:4] - New development model for developing societies stresses **non-material indicators** (quality of life, equity, **wellbeing**).
[113:2:5] - **ILO (2025):** India's social protection coverage **64.3%** (19% in 2015).
[113:2:6] - Dalit change came through state policy, reform movements, Sanskritisation and Westernisation.
[113:2:7] # Theories
[113:2:8] TABLE head: Theory | Proponents
  [113:2:8.0] Evolutionary (linear) | Comte (positivism, three stages, 1830s-40s), Herbert Spencer (simple → complex; coined "survival of the fittest", 1864), L.H. Morgan, Durkheim (mechanical → organic solidarity, *Division of Labour*, 1893)
  [113:2:8.1] Cyclical | Spengler (*Decline of the West*), Toynbee (challenge and response), Sorokin (sensate/ideational), Pareto (circulation of elites)
  [113:2:8.2] Diffusion | Elliot Smith, Perry, Boas
  [113:2:8.3] Technological | Veblen (*Theory of the Leisure Class*), Ogburn (adaptive culture, cultural lag)
  [113:2:8.4] Biological / evolutionary struggle | Darwin – survival of the fittest ("worthy living")
[113:2:9] - **Chronology:** Comte's positivism → Spencer → Durkheim's division of labour.
[113:2:10] - **W.G. Sumner** (*Folkways*, 1906): Social Darwinist; in-group/out-group antagonism and struggle – usually grouped with the early **conflict** school.
[113:2:11] TABLE head: Diffusionist school | Scholars | Idea
  [113:2:11.0] British | Elliot Smith, Perry | Egypt as the source
  [113:2:11.1] German-Austrian | Graebner, Schmidt | Culture circles
  [113:2:11.2] American | Boas, Wissler | Culture areas
[113:2:12] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Society Part 1 p.6-9; app notes 2:113 sub 0-1; general knowledge (Toynbee, Sumner), not checked
## SUB 3 | Westernisation, Modernisation and Secularisation
[113:3:0] # Westernisation (Srinivas)
[113:3:1] - Changes from **150+ years of British rule** in **technology, institutions, ideology, values**; primary, secondary, tertiary Westernisation.
[113:3:2] - Source-specific (West/British) and **ethically neutral**; modernisation is **universal** and value-loaded ("progress").
[113:3:3] - The **English-educated Hindu middle class** was the first to be Westernised.
[113:3:4] # Modernisation
[113:3:5] - **Daniel Lerner**, *The Passing of Traditional Society* (**1958**): **urbanisation → literacy → media exposure → participation**; **"empathy"** = **psychic mobility**.
[113:3:6] - **Yogendra Singh**, *Modernization of Indian Tradition* (**1973**): universalistic, evolutionary cultural response; macro and micro levels.
[113:3:7] - **Milton Singer**, *When a Great Tradition Modernizes*: tradition and modernity **coexist** (Madras temple culture).
[113:3:8] - **Indicators:** rationality, science, industrialisation, urbanisation, literacy, mass media, democratic participation – **not hereditary occupation**.
[113:3:9] - **Zygmunt Bauman – "liquid modernity":** constant **mobility and change in relationships, identities and global economics** in contemporary society.
[113:3:10] # Secularisation
[113:3:11] - Decline of religion's hold on social life; differentiation and **rationalisation**; **Max Weber: "disenchantment of the world"**; Bryan Wilson – decline of organised religious participation; in India, **secularisation of caste** (caste as political pressure group).
[113:3:12] TABLE head: Sociological secularisation | Constitutional secularism
  [113:3:12.0] Change in society | Duty of the state
  [113:3:12.1] Beliefs and practices change | State neutrality and equal respect (Arts. 25-28)
[113:3:13] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Society Part 3 p.14-16; Rocket Indian Society p.14; app notes 2:113 sub 4-5, 7; general knowledge (Bauman), not checked
## SUB 4 | Cultural Lag, Great and Little Traditions, Books
[113:4:0] - **W.F. Ogburn**, *Social Change* (**1922**): **material culture** (technology) changes faster; **non-material culture** trails = **delay in adjustment** = **cultural lag**; "**material culture change lies behind social change**".
[113:4:1] - Lagging parts: **religion, law, tradition** – **not politics**.
[113:4:2] - Example: fast digital spread vs slow rules on children's online safety – **DPDP Act, 2023** (parental consent **under 18**).
[113:4:3] - **Culture** = the sum of human life-ways, behaviour, beliefs, feelings and thought.
[113:4:4] TABLE head: Concept | Originator
  [113:4:4.0] Great Tradition and Little Tradition | Robert Redfield; applied to India by Singer and Marriott
  [113:4:4.1] Universalisation (little → great) and Parochialisation (great → little) | McKim Marriott
  [113:4:4.2] Sanskritisation, Westernisation, Dominant Caste | M.N. Srinivas
[113:4:5] # Books
[113:4:6] TABLE head: Book | Author
  [113:4:6.0] *The Remembered Village*; *Village, Caste, Gender and Method* | M.N. Srinivas
  [113:4:6.1] *Caste and Race in India* | G.S. Ghurye
  [113:4:6.2] *Kinship Organization in India*; *Indian Kinship System* | Irawati Karve
  [113:4:6.3] *Castes in India* (1916); *Annihilation of Caste* (1936); *Who Were the Shudras?* (1946); *The Untouchables* (1948 – origin of untouchability) | B.R. Ambedkar
[113:4:7] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Society p.13-14, p.19; app notes 2:113 sub 6, 8

=== NOTES 2:114 | Social Stratification and Mobility in India
## SUB 0 | Caste as Stratification – Features, Caste vs Class
[114:0:0] # Features of caste
[114:0:1] - Caste membership and status are fixed by **birth** (ascribed); based on the **Chaturvarna** (four-varna) scheme; **hierarchy** is the essence of caste (Dumont).
[114:0:2] - **Essential features:** hierarchy, **endogamy** ("closed marriage", "intermarriage" in Telugu-English papers = marriage within the caste), restrictions on feeding and social intercourse, hereditary occupation, **caste panchayat**, purity-pollution. **Belief in reincarnation** and "social dynamics" are **not** essential features.
[114:0:3] - **Closed system:** a person can **neither rise nor descend** in the hierarchy (A.W. Green: ideally no mobility up or down); caste is a **closed group** that no outsider can join.
[114:0:4] - **Varna** = four-fold, theoretical; **Jati** = real, local birth groups; ranking by **ritual purity and pollution**.
[114:0:5] - **Vertical** classification = ranking by birth; **horizontal** = division into separate caste groups.
[114:0:6] - Caste status is linked to **occupation**; hereditary occupations (potter, **blacksmith**, weaver) weakened by education, **industrialisation**, urbanisation, occupational mobility.
[114:0:7] - **Jajmani system:** barber, washerman etc. are **service castes** working for patron (jajman) families; weakened today.
[114:0:8] - **S.C. Dube:** ritual purity has two stages – **purification procedures** and **initiation rites**.
[114:0:9] - Harappa: citadel vs lower town, **no rigid caste**; varna hardened in the **Later Vedic** period.
[114:0:10] - Today inter-caste conflicts are about **power**, not ritual; Muslims: **Ashraf, Ajlaf, Arzal**.
[114:0:11] # Caste vs class
[114:0:12] TABLE head: System | Feature
  [114:0:12.0] Caste | Ascribed at birth; endogamy, inherited occupation; closed; cumulative inequality
  [114:0:12.1] Class | Achieved – education, wealth, occupation; open, mobility possible
  [114:0:12.2] Estate | Medieval Europe – clergy, nobility, commoners
  [114:0:12.3] Slavery | Person as property – Greece, Rome
[114:0:13] - Both caste and class are forms of stratification and give the individual a status; castes are **innumerable** (only the varnas are four).
[114:0:14] - **Social classes** = people of similar income, occupation, education.
[114:0:15] - **Andre Beteille:** *Caste, Class and Power* (**1965**, **Sripuram, Thanjavur**) – used **Weber's** three dimensions; caste, class and power **diverge**; also *Studies in Agrarian Social Structure*; argued **varna is a hierarchy** term and **race a classification** term.
[114:0:16] - **Louis Dumont**, *Homo Hierarchicus*: purity-pollution; the **Brahman is at the top**, the **king second** (status encompasses power).
[114:0:17] - **Ghurye**, *Caste and Race in India* (1932): hierarchy, endogamy, restrictions.
[114:0:18] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society G2 Part 1 p.2, p.32-35; Rocket Indian Society p.15, p.21-22; app notes 2:114 sub 2; general knowledge (Dube, Beteille on race, Dumont), not checked
[114:0:19] - **We-feeling** is strongest in **primary groups**, above all the **family** (Cooley); class is a loose, impersonal stratum.
## SUB 1 | Stratification – Meaning, Bases, Theories
[114:1:0] - **Stratification:** ranking of groups by unequal **wealth, prestige, power**.
[114:1:1] - **Bases:** caste, class, **gender (sex stratification = between genders)**, **age**, race, ethnicity; traditional – caste, varna, tribe, religion; modern – education, occupation, income, **political power**, urbanisation. **Language is NOT** a basis.
[114:1:2] - **Differentiation vs stratification:** **sex** (biological) is differentiation; class, caste, gender are stratification.
[114:1:3] - **Tumin:** stratification is social, **ancient, universal**, diverse, **consequential** (decides life chances).
[114:1:4] TABLE head: Approach | Thinker | Idea
  [114:1:4.0] Functionalist | Davis and Moore (1945) | Unequal rewards pull scarce talent into key posts
  [114:1:4.1] Critique | Melvin Tumin | Wastes talent; passes inequality on
  [114:1:4.2] Conflict | Marx | Ownership of means of production; class struggle; false consciousness hides the real status of the oppressed
  [114:1:4.3] Multi-dimensional | Weber | Class, status, party (power/authority); market situation decides life chances
  [114:1:4.4] Ideological | Dumont | Purity-pollution
[114:1:5] # Terms
[114:1:6] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [114:1:6.0] Status inconsistency (Lenski) | Different ranks on different dimensions
  [114:1:6.1] Status group (Weber; "floor group" in translation) | Shared lifestyle; caste = a closed status group
  [114:1:6.2] Life chances (Weber) | Access to necessities, opportunities
[114:1:7] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Society p.21-22; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Society Part 1 p.13-14; app notes 2:114 sub 0-1, 7
## SUB 2 | Social Mobility – Types and Examples
[114:2:0] - **Social mobility** = **movement of people between social strata/positions**.
[114:2:1] TABLE head: Type | Meaning / example
  [114:2:1.0] Vertical (upward/downward) | Farmer's son → IAS officer
  [114:2:1.1] Horizontal | Change without status change: clerk to an equal job; change of religion (an untouchable converting to Christianity – Sorokin)
  [114:2:1.2] Inter-generational | Parents → children: labourer's/farmer's son → engineer
  [114:2:1.3] Intra-generational | Within one lifetime
  [114:2:1.4] Structural | Change in the occupational structure itself
[114:2:2] - **Sorokin**, *Social Mobility* (**1927**): first set out vertical and horizontal mobility.
[114:2:3] - **Bogardus:** social mobility as **change on the same status level** (APPSC Hostel Welfare key).
[114:2:4] # Status and role
[114:2:5] - **Ascribed status:** given at birth – **sex, age, caste**, race, kinship; **achieved**: IAS officer, doctor.
[114:2:6] - **Status set:** the many statuses one person holds; **role** = the behaviour pattern of the rights and duties of a status ("status is occupied, roles are played").
[114:2:7] - Paired statuses such as **husband-wife, guru-disciple** – reciprocal statuses (APPSC key: "processing status").
[114:2:8] - **Dominant caste** (Srinivas): **numerical strength**, sizeable **arable land (economic power)**, **political power**, fairly **high ritual rank**; later western education and administrative jobs.
[114:2:9] - **Kshatriyaisation (Hermann Kulke):** Marathas, Jats, Yadavs claim Kshatriya status – mobility that **reproduces the hierarchy**.
[114:2:10] - **Nomadic society:** marked by moving from place to place (migration).
[114:2:11] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Society p.18, p.23; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Society Part 1 p.14-15; app notes 2:114 sub 3; general knowledge (Sorokin on religion, Bogardus), not checked
## SUB 3 | Agrarian Classes and Middle Class
[114:3:0] - **Daniel Thorner:** by land rights and income – **Maliks** (landlords on rent), **Kisans** (own land, family labour), **Mazdoors** (tenants, sharecroppers, landless).
[114:3:1] - Dominant caste is a concept for **stratification in rural India**.
[114:3:2] - **Macaulay's Minute, 1835** → English-educated middle class (**A.R. Desai**, *Social Background of Indian Nationalism*).
[114:3:3] - Middle class: World Bank **$10-50**/day (PPP); NCAER **₹2-10 lakh**; PRICE **₹5-30 lakh**; **43.2 crore (31%) in 2021 → 61% by 2047**; OECD: world's largest by **2035**.
[114:3:4] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Society p.14; NextGen Society G2 Part 1 p.39-40; app notes 2:114 sub 4-5
## SUB 4 | Mobility Routes, OBCs and Andhra
[114:4:0] - **ES 2025-26:** drivers – **health, education, technology, institutions** (not land inheritance); low mobility **entrenches historical inequality**; poverty **21.9% (2011-12) → 2.3% (2023-24)**.
[114:4:1] - **Mandal Commission:** OBCs **over 52%**; **11 indicators = 4 social + 4 economic + 3 educational** (social, economic, educational categories).
[114:4:2] - **Telangana caste survey:** **242 castes**; **135** above average backwardness.
[114:4:3] - **Marathas, Gujjars, Patels** seek OBC status mainly for **greater life chances**.
[114:4:4] - Reservation demand: **Periyar's Self-Respect Movement**; **Ezhavas** (Kerala): toddy tapping → tailoring (occupational mobility); city anonymity weakens caste.
[114:4:5] - **Dalits:** state policy, reform movements, Sanskritisation and Westernisation.
[114:4:6] - **Medieval Andhra:** **Kakatiya** society relatively open (**Velamas, Kammas, Reddys** rose); **Saivism (Virashaivism)** a "**lubricant**" of upward mobility.
[114:4:7] ~~ Sources: app notes 2:114 sub 6; NextGen Society G2 Part 2 p.35

=== NOTES 2:115 | Rural, Urban and Tribal Society in India – Features and Interlinkages
## SUB 0 | Rural Community and Village Studies
[115:0:0] # The village as a unit
[115:0:1] - **Rural sociology:** the study of rural society – its **social structure, institutions, change and conflict** in villages.
[115:0:2] - **Elements of a rural community:** **territory, we-feeling, relative self-sufficiency, small size, homogeneity**.
[115:0:3]   - **⚠ Trap:** **cultural diversity** is NOT a rural element; diversity and heterogeneity are urban (UPPSC 2021).
[115:0:4] - **Charles Metcalfe:** villages as self-reliant **"little republics"**.
[115:0:5] - **Robert Redfield**, *The Little Community* (1955): the village as a **"little community"** with four traits – **distinctiveness, smallness, homogeneity, self-sufficiency** (TSPSC 2023; CSP 2002). Tonnies = Gemeinschaft-Gesellschaft; Maine = "village communities".
[115:0:6] - **Myth of self-sufficiency:** **M.N. Srinivas and A.M. Shah** ("The Myth of the Self-Sufficiency of the Indian Village", 1960) – villages depended on outside markets; Srinivas debunked villages as unchanging, self-sufficient "little republics".
[115:0:7] - **Andre Beteille** (1980): "the village was not merely a place where people lived; it had a **design** in which were reflected the **basic values of Indian civilisation**".
[115:0:8] - **S.C. Dube:** argued for **systematic study of village communities for better planning**; his Shamirpet study (Osmania University project) was a laboratory for rural development programmes.
[115:0:9] # Village studies
[115:0:10] TABLE head: Village | Scholar
  [115:0:10.0] Rampura (Mysore) | M.N. Srinivas, *The Remembered Village*
  [115:0:10.1] Shamirpet (near Hyderabad) | S.C. Dube, *Indian Village* (1955)
  [115:0:10.2] Kishan Garhi (UP) | McKim Marriott
  [115:0:10.3] Senapur (Jaunpur) | Opler, R.D. Singh, Bernard Cohn
  [115:0:10.4] Sripuram (Thanjavur) | Andre Beteille
  [115:0:10.5] Karimpur (UP) | William and Charlotte Wiser, *Behind Mud Walls*
[115:0:11] > Who-said angle (TSPSC CDPO 2023 ×4): myth of self-sufficiency = Srinivas & Shah; "design of Indian civilisation" = Beteille; planning-oriented village study = Dube; little community = Redfield.
[115:0:12] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Society Part 1 l.1364-1375; Part 4 p.5 l.196-214; web: qeh.ox.ac.uk working paper 5 (Beteille quote); app notes 2:115 sub 0; general knowledge (Redfield, Srinivas-Shah 1960)
## SUB 1 | Village Economy – Jajmani, Peasants and Agrarian Society
[115:1:0] # Jajmani system
[115:1:1] - **Jajmani:** a socio-economic and ritual arrangement in which one caste secures the service of another; each works for a family with whom it is **hereditarily linked** – between landholder patron (**jajman**) and service castes (**kamin**).
[115:1:2] - **Exchange by tradition:** goods and services pass by **custom and tradition**, not law or market value of goods.
[115:1:3] - **Features:** **functional reciprocity** between castes within the **village social structure**; the **Mahalwari system** is a British land-revenue settlement, not a jajmani feature (CSP 1998).
[115:1:4] - **First scientific study:** **William Wiser**, *The Hindu Jajmani System* (1936), a UP village.
[115:1:5] # Peasants and agrarian society
[115:1:6] - **Peasant (rythu, kisan):** **owns/holds land and cultivates it with the labour of family members** (Thorner's kisan); one who cultivates only through hired labour is a landlord-farmer.
[115:1:7] - **Agricultural vs industrial society:** differ in **premises, method of production and social dynamics** – all of these.
[115:1:8] - Forms of exchange (Polanyi): **reciprocity, redistribution, market exchange**; "antagonism" is not a form of exchange.
[115:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society Group 2 Part 3 p.35; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Society Part 4 p.5; general knowledge (Wiser 1936, Thorner, Polanyi)
## SUB 2 | Urban Society and Census Data
[115:2:0] - Urban life: **competition, impersonal relations, anonymity, weak control** – **not informal ties** (JPSC 2021).
[115:2:1] - **Louis Wirth**, *Urbanism as a Way of Life* (**1938**): **size, density, heterogeneity**.
[115:2:2] - **Urbanism** = social-cultural side; **urbanisation** = population shift.
[115:2:3] - **Urban area** = statutory towns (Municipality, Corporation, Cantonment Board, Notified Town Area Committee) + census towns.
[115:2:4] - **Census town:** **5,000** people; **75%** (not 60%) of male main workers non-farm; **400/sq km**; unchanged since **1981**; kept for **Census 2027** (17 Sep 2026), though MoHUA called it outdated.
[115:2:5] - Urban share **11% (1901) → 27.81% (2001) → 31.16% (2011)**; centres 1,827 → 7,935.
[115:2:6] - **2001-11 urban jump:** mainly **reclassification** of villages as census towns (about **2,500** added); urban share 31.1%.
[115:2:7] - **Largest UAs (2001):** **Greater Mumbai > Kolkata > Delhi**; by 2011 Delhi passed Kolkata.
[115:2:8] - 2011: **68.8% rural**, **6,40,867 villages**.
[115:2:9] - **Hidden urbanisation** (DEGURBA): ~**63%** urban (2015).
[115:2:10] - **16th FC (2026-31):** ULB grant share **36% → 45%**; 41% urban by 2031.
[115:2:11] > Census criteria angle: "60% of male workers non-agricultural" is the wrong criterion – it is 75%.
[115:2:12] ~~ Sources: app notes 2:115 sub 2 (Census 2011, ES 2025-26, 16th FC); general knowledge (Wirth)
## SUB 3 | Rural-urban Continuum and Urbanisation
[115:3:0] - **Redfield:** **folk-urban continuum** (Mexico, **Yucatan**) – a gradual scale, not two boxes.
[115:3:1] TABLE head: Feature | Village | Town/City
  [115:3:1.0] Occupation | Agriculture | Non-agricultural
  [115:3:1.1] Size | Small, sparse | Large, dense
  [115:3:1.2] Relations | Primary, face-to-face | Secondary, impersonal
  [115:3:1.3] Control | Informal (caste, custom) | Formal (law, police)
[115:3:2] - Village-to-town transition begins with **traders and manufacturers** (not wholly dependent on village resources).
[115:3:3] # Primary vs secondary urbanisation
[115:3:4] TABLE head: Primary | Secondary
  [115:3:4.0] Orthogenetic | Heterogenetic
  [115:3:4.1] Folk culture → Great Tradition | New thought replaces old
  [115:3:4.2] Moral order (temple centres) | Technical order
[115:3:5] - Typology: **Redfield and Singer**; **Singer** studied Madras Hinduism. **Marriott:** universalisation and parochialisation.
[115:3:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 2:115 sub 1, 3
## SUB 4 | Urban Problems and Migration
[115:4:0] - **Industrialisation** drives urbanisation; **density** raises **crime**; maladjustment, rich-poor segregation, alienation.
[115:4:1] - **ES 2025-26:** informality (slums, informal labour) is **structural** – integrate, not eradicate; cities lack **fiscal autonomy**; **35%** rural households lack healthcare within 5 km.
[115:4:2] - Caste persists through slums and job networks.
[115:4:3] - **Jockin (Joachim) Arputham:** Magsaysay awardee (2000); President of the **National Slum Dwellers' Federation**; accompanied **Prince Charles** in **Dharavi** (Mumbai), among Asia's largest slums (5 Nov 2003).
[115:4:4] # Migration
[115:4:5] - **Jan Breman**, *Footloose Labour* (**1996**): circular migrants in seasonal, casual, informal jobs.
[115:4:6] - Sources: **UP, Bihar**; push: monsoon failure, unemployment; urban wages **1.7-2x** rural.
[115:4:7] - **SPMRM (2016):** "rural soul, urban amenities"; **PMEGP** (KVIC).
[115:4:8] ~~ Sources: app notes 2:115 sub 4, 6; general knowledge (Arputham)
## SUB 5 | Tribal Society
[115:5:0] - Features: common **name, dialect**, territory, ancestor, **animism/totemism**, clans, **youth dormitories**, simple economy.
[115:5:1] TABLE head: Tribe | Peasant
  [115:5:1.0] Isolated, kinship-based, egalitarian | Part of wider caste-class society
  [115:5:1.1] Common land and forest | Market-linked; individual land
[115:5:2] - **N.K. Bose:** Hindu method of tribal absorption; **Surajit Sinha:** **tribe-caste model (continuum)** of tribal amalgamation (CSP 1999); **T.K. Oommen:** tribal autonomy.
[115:5:3] - 1960s debate: tribes as one end of a continuum with caste-based peasant society vs a wholly distinct type (no purity-pollution).
[115:5:4] - STs: **89.97% rural**; **705** groups.
[115:5:5] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Society Part 1 l.1870-1901; app notes 2:115 sub 5

  [115:6:0.0] Urban share | 24.13% (2001) → 29.47% (2011); ~70.5% rural
  [115:6:0.1] Most urban (old 13) | Visakhapatnam 47.45%, Krishna 40.81%
  [115:6:0.2] Least urban | Srikakulam 16.16%

  [115:6:0.4] Largest rural population | East Godavari
  [115:6:0.5] 28 districts (2025-26) | Visakhapatnam 89.69%; Polavaram 2.84%
  [115:6:0.6] STs | 27.39 lakh (5.53%); 34 communities
  [115:6:0.7] Scheduled Areas | 16,267.63 sq km, 3,512 villages; ~12.9 lakh STs
[115:6:1] - Scheduled Area districts: **Parvathipuram Manyam, Vizianagaram, Alluri Sitarama Raju, Anakapalli, Eluru**.
[115:6:2] - Urban population 173.5 lakh → 190.9 lakh (2029).

=== NOTES 2:120 | Regionalism in Andhra Pradesh – Regional Imbalance and Its Politics
## SUB 0 | Capital City Debate
[120:0:0] TABLE head: Capital (2020 plan) | City
  [120:0:0.0] Executive | Visakhapatnam
  [120:0:0.1] Legislative | Amaravati
  [120:0:0.2] Judicial | Kurnool
[120:0:1] - **2020:** **AP Decentralisation and Inclusive Development of All Regions Act, 2020** + **APCRDA (Repeal) Act, 2020**.
[120:0:2] - **Nov 2021:** Repeal Bill introduced in the AP Assembly; both Acts **withdrawn (2021)**.
[120:0:3] - **31 Jan 2023:** CM Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy declared **Visakhapatnam** the capital.
[120:0:4] - **2026:** the Lok Sabha passed the **AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026**, formally declaring **Amaravati the (sole) capital** after the 10-year joint-capital period ended.
[120:0:5] - **Amaravati:** planned to be built in **three phases**; **M. Swarajyamma** is cited as the first lady to donate **₹1 crore** for its construction (APPSC PYQ).
[120:0:6] - **Jan 2026:** coalition govt committed to finishing Amaravati in three years; seeks a central law to protect it. **1 Feb 2026:** CII AP sought a special package for Amaravati.
[120:0:7] - YSRCP view: Amaravati spending hurts north coastal and drought-prone Rayalaseema.
[120:0:8] - Compare: **Kalyana Karnataka** – **Art. 371J** (since 2013); disparities continue.
[120:0:9] ~~ Sources: CARE APPSC Apr 2026 p.5 (AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026); app notes 2:120 sub 5; Amaravati phases and donor: printed PYQ answers, not verified
## SUB 1 | Committees on Regional Imbalance
[120:1:0] TABLE head: Committee | Year | Mandate
  [120:1:0.0] Bhargava | 1969 | Telangana surplus funds diverted to other regions
  [120:1:0.1] Wanchoo | 1969 | Ways to keep Mulki (employment) safeguards
  [120:1:0.2] Srikrishna (Justice B.N. Srikrishna) | 2010 | Telangana / united AP question; six options (Dec 2010)
  [120:1:0.3] Sivaramakrishnan (K.C. Sivaramakrishnan) | 2014 | Under the AP Reorganisation Act – site of new capital
[120:1:1] - **Srikrishna Committee (Feb 2010):** set up **on the question of Telangana State**.
[120:1:2] # Srikrishna Committee findings
[120:1:3] - **First option:** keep AP **as it is (status quo)** – found least workable; the six options ranged from status quo to bifurcation.
[120:1:4] - **Nature of the demand:** a desire for **greater democracy and empowerment** – **greater political space and power** within a political unit.
[120:1:5] - **Per capita income growth 2000-01 to 2007-08:** highest in **Telangana excluding Hyderabad (60.3%)**; 63% with Hyderabad; Rayalaseema 58%; Coastal Andhra 54.1%.
[120:1:6] - **Urbanisation 1961-2001:** highest growth in **Telangana** (Hyderabad-led).
[120:1:7] - Telangana (excluding Hyderabad) on par with or a shade lower than Coastal Andhra on most indicators; far better once Hyderabad is included.
[120:1:8] ~~ Sources: web: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Srikrishna_Committee; sujaiblog.blogspot.com (The Hindu on the report's income data); app notes 2:120 sub 3
## SUB 2 | AP Reorganisation Act, 2014
[120:2:0] - **Appointed day: 2 June 2014** – AP and Telangana became separate States (Telangana = 29th State); **Hyderabad** common capital for up to **10 years**.
[120:2:1] - **Sec. 46(2)-(3):** backward-areas package; **Sec. 94:** tax incentives.
[120:2:2] - **7 backward districts** = 4 Rayalaseema + 3 North Andhra; grant of **₹50 crore per district per year**.
[120:2:3] - **SCS:** PM promised in Rajya Sabha (**Feb 2014**); **14th Finance Commission** ended the general/special distinction → "**special assistance measure**"; demand still a political issue.
[120:2:4] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Part 1 l.4683; app notes 2:120 sub 4
## SUB 3 | Mulki Rules, Six Point Formula and Movements
[120:3:0] - **Jai Andhra movement (1972):** reaction to the Supreme Court **upholding Mulki rules**; sought separate Andhra; started in Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema.
[120:3:1] - **Six Point Formula (21 Sept 1973)** → **32nd Amendment, 1973** inserted **Article 371D** – the **special provision for Andhra Pradesh** (zonal system of local cadres, education and employment) and **371E**; ended the Regional Committee (Art. 371(1)).
[120:3:2] - **8-Point Formula (1969):** set up a high-level committee under a judge and a special committee on Telangana surpluses.
[120:3:3] - **Telangana movements:** 1969 agitation; 2009-14 phase → Telangana State 2014.
[120:3:4] - **⚠ Trap:** Capital-location committee came under the **2014 Act**, not the 8-Point Formula.
[120:3:5] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Part 2 l.18556 (Art. 371D); app notes 2:120 sub 2
## SUB 4 | Regions and Employment Zones
[120:4:0] TABLE head: Zone (pre-2022, 13 districts) | Districts
  [120:4:0.0] Zone I – North Andhra (Uttarandhra) | Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam
  [120:4:0.1] Zone II | East Godavari, West Godavari, Krishna
  [120:4:0.2] Zone III | Guntur, Prakasam, Nellore (Coastal Andhra, not North Andhra)
  [120:4:0.3] Zone IV – Rayalaseema | Kurnool, Anantapur, Kadapa (YSR district), Chittoor
  [120:4:0.4] Zones V, VI | Went to Telangana
[120:4:1] - Coastal Andhra (esp. **Krishna-Guntur**) is more developed than North Andhra and Rayalaseema.
[120:4:2] - **Per capita income (2025-26 AE):** **Visakhapatnam** top (₹6,58,964), Krishna next; **no Rayalaseema district** reaches the State average (₹2,94,507); **Kurnool** lowest.
[120:4:3] - **Rainfall:** **Anantapur 544 mm** vs up to 1,250 mm in Srikakulam-Vizianagaram. AP literacy (2011): **67.35%**.
[120:4:4] - **Jan 2026:** NITI Aayog monitors **112 Aspirational Districts**; AP Cabinet tracked **₹8.55 lakh crore** investment for jobs in North Andhra and Rayalaseema.
[120:4:5] - **Rayalaseema industrial hub (Jul 2026):** **JSW steel – Kadapa**; **Royal Enfield – Tirupati**; Kia plant; proposed **Space City** near Sriharikota.
[120:4:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 2:120 sub 0
## SUB 5 | Historical Agreements
[120:5:0] - **Sri Bagh Pact (16 Nov 1937):** first Coastal-Rayalaseema accord; drafted by **Pattabhi Sitaramayya**; Rayalaseema to choose **either the capital or the High Court**; aimed to raise Rayalaseema's farm and economic level to coastal districts. Andhra State capital → **Kurnool** (1953).
[120:5:1] - **Gentlemen's Agreement – 1956** (not 1969): reused the Sri Bagh template for Telangana safeguards.
[120:5:2] - Such pacts institutionalised sub-regional fault lines; poor implementation fed agitations.
[120:5:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 2:120 sub 1

## SUB 4 | Forms
[121:4:0] - Student agitations and protests; **secessionist** (Naga, Assam, Khalistan).
[121:4:1] - **Militancy:** **Dalit Panthers** – militant Dalit youth organisation formed in **Maharashtra (1972)**; deviance: **drug abuse**.
[121:4:2] - **New pattern:** **leaderless, digital** protests on encrypted apps, no formal central committee (Bangladesh 2024, Nepal Gen Z 2025).
[121:4:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society G2 Part 3 p.42 l.2190 (Dalit Panthers); app notes 2:121 sub 2
## SUB 5 | Meaning, Types and Theories
[121:5:0] - **Deviance:** behaviour that **violates the norms** of a group or society (crime = law-breaking deviance).
[121:5:1] - **Youth unrest:** collective frustration among young people when society's norms seem **ineffective or harmful**.
[121:5:2] TABLE head: Type | Example
  [121:5:2.0] Persuasive | Exam postponement
  [121:5:2.1] Resistance | Against attendance rules
  [121:5:2.2] Revolutionary | Overthrow the system (AASU, Bodo)
[121:5:3] - **Life cycle:** **Discontent** (first) → initiation → formalisation → public support → official action.
[121:5:4] - **Theories:** discontent; **personal maladjustment**; **relative deprivation (Stouffer)**; **resource mobilisation** (tactics and leadership matter more than grievances).
[121:5:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 2:121 sub 0; general knowledge (deviance)
## SUB 6 | Causes
[121:6:0] - **Unemployment / jobless growth:** about **9.7 million** join the working-age group each year (2021-31).
[121:6:1] - **Educational mismatch**, capitation fees; **identity crisis** and **generation gap** as families become nuclear; **political interference**.
[121:6:2] TABLE head: Campus causes | Off-campus causes
  [121:6:2.0] Exams, fees, hostels, teacher tensions | Sympathetic strikes, political interference, wider issues (CAA/NRC)
[121:6:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 2:121 sub 1
## SUB 7 | Demographics and Unemployment Data
[121:7:0] - **Census 2011:** youth (15-24) about **231 million**, **~19.1%** of population; demographic dividend needs jobs for the 9.7 million yearly entrants.

  [121:7:1.0] India 15-29 (MoSPI 2022) | Male 13.0%, female 12.5%
  [121:7:1.1] India 15-29 (PLFS 2025 annual) | 9.9% (from 10.3%); urban 13.6%, rural 8.3%
  [121:7:1.2] AP (PLFS 2023-24) | Youth 17.5% (above national); rural 15.5%, urban 22.7%; urban female 29.1%
  [121:7:1.3] Global (ILO 2026) | 12.4% (67 M); NEET 20%; women 27.4% vs men 13.1%
[121:7:2] - **Adolescents (Census 2011):** about **253 million** people aged **10-19**, about **20.9%** of the population (UNFPA).

=== NOTES 2:122 | Other Social Problems – Alcoholism, Drug Abuse, Suicide, Beggary and Human Trafficking
## SUB 0 | Suicide – Durkheim's Types and NCRB Data
[122:0:0] # Durkheim's types (*Le Suicide*, 1897)
[122:0:1] TABLE head: Type | Cause | Example
  [122:0:1.0] Egoistic | Too little integration | Isolated individual
  [122:0:1.1] Altruistic | Too much integration – the group demands the death | Sati (obligatory altruistic), hara-kiri
  [122:0:1.2] Anomic | Too little regulation (crisis, sudden change, normlessness) | Economic crash
  [122:0:1.3] Fatalistic | Too much regulation | Slaves, harshly ruled persons
[122:0:2] - **Sati = altruistic suicide**, not anomic; "passive" and "self-respect" suicide are not Durkheim's types (APPSC Sociology 2000: answer "None of the above" when altruistic is not printed).
[122:0:3] - **Durkheim's *Le Suicide*:** published in **1897**; anomie = normlessness caused by rapid social change.
[122:0:4] # NCRB ADSI data
[122:0:5] - **ADSI 2015 – farmer suicides:** **bankruptcy/indebtedness** first (**38.7%**), then **farming-related issues** (19.5%) (**APPSC G1 2017**).
[122:0:6] - **ADSI 2024** (NCRB, released May 2026): **1,70,746 suicides**; **daily wagers ~31%**; homemakers 22,113; unemployed 14,778; students 14,488; **drug-overdose deaths 978 (up 50%)**.
[122:0:7] - **Top States (ADSI 2024):** **Maharashtra** (**22,174**, about 13%), then **Tamil Nadu** (19,965) and **Madhya Pradesh** (15,491).
[122:0:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Society #14 p.46; web: open.oregonstate.education (Ellis review of Durkheim: suttee = altruistic); web: ecologise.in (ADSI 2015 shares); app notes 2:122 sub 0 (ADSI 2024 figures, not re-checked; release date per Rocket CA 2026-01 p.19)
## SUB 1 | Attempt to Suicide in Law
[122:1:0] TABLE head: Law / case | Provision
  [122:1:0.0] Sec. 309 IPC | Attempt punishable with simple imprisonment up to one year and/or fine
  [122:1:0.1] P. Rathinam (1994) | Held Sec. 309 invalid (later overruled in Gian Kaur, 1996)
  [122:1:0.2] Law Commission, 210th Report | Recommended deleting Sec. 309
  [122:1:0.3] Mental Healthcare Act 2017, Sec. 115 | Presumes severe stress → no trial or punishment; State must provide care
  [122:1:0.4] BNS 2023 (in force 1 July 2024) | No general attempted-suicide offence; Sec. 226 = attempt to suicide to coerce a public servant
[122:1:1] - **Suicide** is the crime whose **attempt** was punishable but whose **completion** cannot be punished (the culprit is dead); murder, theft, rape are punishable either way (MPPSC 1991).
[122:1:2] - **Tele-MANAS:** tele-mental-health helpline, launched **10 Oct 2022**, toll-free **14416**.
[122:1:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 2:122 sub 1; Praveen CA360 Mar 2026 magazine (Tele-MANAS 14416, MHCA 2017); general knowledge (Gian Kaur, BNS 226), not checked
## SUB 2 | Human Trafficking
[122:2:0] - **Meaning:** trade in humans for sexual slavery, forced labour or commercial sexual exploitation – a form of **modern slavery**.
[122:2:1] - **Article 23 (Fundamental Right – Right against Exploitation)** prohibits **traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour** – it is **NOT a Directive Principle** (UPSC 2008).
[122:2:2] - **Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956** (SITA 1956, renamed ITPA in 1986) is the main law on sex trafficking; **BNS Sec. 143** defines trafficking; also POCSO 2012, Bonded Labour (Abolition) Act 1976; India signed the **Palermo Protocol**.
[122:2:3] - **Most cases – West Bengal:** NCRB *Crime in India 2016*: **West Bengal 3,579 cases (~44%)**, then Rajasthan (1,422).
[122:2:4] - **Anti Human Trafficking Units (AHTUs):** **696** across States/UTs (NCRB *Crime in India 2020*); ~2,183 trafficking cases in 2023 (NCRB).
[122:2:5] - UNODC: India is both a **high-origin and high-destination** country.
[122:2:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society G2 Part 3 p.37; PMF Lens Apr 2026 p.9; Laxmikanth 8th ed. (Art. 23); web: fighttrafficking.org (NCRB 2016); app notes 2:122 sub 5
## SUB 3 | Beggary
[122:3:0] - **West Bengal** tops the Social Justice Ministry's Census 2011 list of beggars and vagrants (**81,224**), then **UP** (65,835), **AP** (30,218), **Bihar** (29,723); India total **4,13,670** (BPSC 2017).
[122:3:1] - **Bombay Prevention of Begging Act, 1959**: punitive model copied by many States.
[122:3:2] - **Delhi HC (2018, Harsh Mander)**: **decriminalised begging** in Delhi.
[122:3:3] - **SC (2021)**: refused to ban begging; a **socio-economic problem**.
[122:3:4] - **SMILE (MoSJE, 2022)**: sub-scheme for **comprehensive rehabilitation of persons engaged in begging** ("Bhiksha Vritti Mukt Bharat"); rights-based, not punitive; 216 cities, target 295 by 2030-31.
[122:3:5] - **Indore**: **first officially beggar-free city (2025)**.
[122:3:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Lens Jul 2026 p.63-64 (SMILE, Indore); web: gktoday.in (Lok Sabha reply, beggars by State); app notes 2:122 sub 2
## SUB 4 | Alcoholism
[122:4:0] - **Art. 47 (DPSP)**: State to prohibit **intoxicating drinks** and drugs injurious to health **except for medicinal purposes**.
[122:4:1] - **Health effect:** chronic alcohol and drug use → **liver cirrhosis** and **nervous-system damage** (not leukaemia/lymphoma).
[122:4:2] - **Anti-Arrack Movement**: began **1992**, **Dubagunta** village, **Nellore** district (not Nizamabad); neo-literate women of the literacy campaign; led by **Dubagunta Rosamma**.
[122:4:3] - Precedent: **R. Venkataratnam Naidu's Social Purity Association (1891)**, a temperance campaign.
[122:4:4] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. (DPSP, Art. 47); PMF General Science 05 p.5 (cirrhosis); app notes 2:122 sub 3
## SUB 5 | Drug Abuse
[122:5:0] - India lies between the **Golden Crescent** and **Golden Triangle**.
[122:5:1] - **National Survey on Extent and Pattern of Substance Use (2019, MoSJE with AIIMS-NDDTC)**: **alcohol 14.6%** → **cannabis 2.8%** → opioids 2.1%.
[122:5:2] TABLE head: Campaign | Ministry / year | Key point
  [122:5:2.0] Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan | MoSJE, 15 Aug 2020 | First 272 districts, now all; implemented by NISD; NMBA 2.0 app

## SUB 6 | Jogini (Devadasi) System
[122:6:0] - **Jogini/Devadasi/Basavi:** dedication of girls (mostly Dalit) to a village deity, leading to sexual exploitation – a form of trafficking and social evil.
[122:6:1] - **Law:** **AP Devadasis (Prohibition of Dedication) Act, 1988/89**; AP rehabilitates Jogin women through APSCCFC economic-support schemes.
[122:6:2] - **Most prevalent (Telangana):** old **Mahbubnagar** district (about **2,000 Joginis**); also Nizamabad, Medak, Adilabad; only marginal in Karimnagar, Warangal, Khammam.

=== NOTES 2:123 | Poverty, Unemployment and Social Exclusion As Social Problems
## SUB 0 | MGNREGA and the VB-G RAM G Act
[123:0:0] TABLE head: Event | Date
  [123:0:0.0] NREGA passed by Parliament | August 2005 (assent September 2005)
  [123:0:0.1] In force | 2 February 2006, launched in Anantapur district (AP); all districts from 1 April 2008
  [123:0:0.2] Renamed MGNREGA | 2 October 2009
  [123:0:0.3] VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 | Passed 18 Dec 2025; in force 1 July 2026, replacing MGNREGA
[123:0:1] # Provisions (MGNREGA)
[123:0:2] - **Legal right** to at least **100 days** of unskilled wage work in a **financial year** per **rural household**; **adult members of any rural household** willing to do unskilled manual work are eligible (not only SC/ST/BPL).
[123:0:3] - Aim: guarantee the **"Right to Work"**; livelihood security, durable assets, **strengthening the livelihood resource base of the poor**, **proactive social inclusion**, **strengthening PRIs** – not higher education.
[123:0:4] - Work within **5 km**; no work within **15 days** of demand → **unemployment allowance**.
[123:0:5] - At least **one-third** of workers must be **women** (not half).
[123:0:6] - **Gram Sabha:** recommends works, monitors them, holds **social audits**; **Gram Panchayat** registers households, **receives work applications and issues dated receipts**.
[123:0:7] - Follows the **Directive Principles** (Art. 41); the right to work is **not** in Part III (Fundamental Rights).
[123:0:8] # VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (now)
[123:0:9] - **Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin)**; Ministry of Rural Development.
[123:0:10] - **125 days** per rural household per year; wage floor **₹300/day** (2026-27); funding **60:40** (NE/Himalayan 90:10).
[123:0:11] - **AP ranked first** in implementation (2.10 crore person-days in the first 45 days).
[123:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 01 p.57; Rocket CA 2026-01 p.156; PMF Lens Jul 2026 p.61; Praveen CA360 Aug 2026 p.35; app notes 2:123 sub 6
## SUB 1 | Poverty and Employment Programmes – Chronology
[123:1:0] TABLE head: Year | Programme | Feature
  [123:1:0.0] 1972 | Maharashtra EGS | First employment guarantee scheme (state level)
  [123:1:0.1] 1978-79 / 2 Oct 1980 | IRDP | Self-employment through subsidy and credit for rural BPL
  [123:1:0.2] 15 Aug 1979 | TRYSEM | Training rural youth for self-employment; component of IRDP
  [123:1:0.3] 1980 | NREP | Rural wage employment (replaced Food for Work)
  [123:1:0.4] 1982-83 | DWCRA | Sub-scheme of IRDP so that benefits reach rural women
  [123:1:0.5] 1989 | JRY | Merged NREP and RLEGP; wage employment
  [123:1:0.6] 1 April 1999 | SGSY | Merged IRDP, TRYSEM, DWCRA (and others); SHG-based self-employment
  [123:1:0.7] 2005 / 2006 | NREGA | Legal guarantee of wage work
  [123:1:0.8] 2008 | PMEGP | Merged PMRY and REGP; credit-linked subsidy through KVIC
  [123:1:0.9] 2011 | NRLM "Aajeevika" (DAY-NRLM from 2016) | Restructured SGSY; SHG livelihoods
[123:1:1] - **Order:** IRDP → NREP → JRY → SGSY → NRLM. DAY-NRLM restructured **SGSY**, NOT JRY.
[123:1:2] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.4, p.51; NextGen Indian Economy P1 04 p.25, p.57; app notes 2:123 sub 5
## SUB 2 | Social Exclusion
[123:2:0] - **Meaning:** a **process** that shuts people out of **facilities, benefits and opportunities** that others enjoy; it is **involuntary and systematic** (NCERT).
[123:2:1] - Term coined by **René Lenoir** (France, **1974**).
[123:2:2] TABLE head: Basis | Example
  [123:2:2.0] Caste | Untouchability against SCs
  [123:2:2.1] Gender | Denial of property, work, mobility
  [123:2:2.2] Race / tribe | Adivasis in remote areas, racial discrimination
  [123:2:2.3] Disability | Lack of access to schools, jobs; segregated special schools
  [123:2:2.4] Religion / region | Minorities; backward, remote areas
[123:2:3] - **All of caste, gender, race and tribe** are bases of exclusion (TSPSC 2018).
[123:2:4] - **Practices leading to exclusion:** **untouchability**, **segregation** (e.g. a **special school for the blind** instead of inclusive schooling), denied access to **land, water and jobs**. MGNREGA wage work is a remedy, not a practice of exclusion.
[123:2:5] - **Results:** hurts **human-capital development**, **widens inequalities**, drives **social unrest and crime** – it does **not** bridge historical divisions (TSPSC 2023).
[123:2:6] # Constitutional remedies
[123:2:7] - **Reservations** for SCs, STs, OBCs aim at **social justice and equal opportunity**.
[123:2:8] - **Art. 46 (DPSP):** promotion of **educational and economic interests** of SCs, STs and other weaker sections.
[123:2:9] - **10 Aug 2026:** the Union **opposes a creamy layer for SCs/STs**, since income alone does not end caste-based exclusion.
[123:2:10] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Society 02 p.1; NextGen Society G2 Part 3 p.36; NextGen Society G2 Part 1 p.66; Laxmikanth 8th ed. (Art. 46); app notes 2:123 sub 7
## SUB 3 | Poverty – Concepts, Causes and Indicators
[123:3:0] TABLE head: Concept | Meaning | Measured by
  [123:3:0.0] Absolute poverty | Spending below the minimum for basic needs | A fixed poverty line (MPCE cut-off)
  [123:3:0.1] Relative poverty | Being poor compared with others in the same society | Inequality / share of income
  [123:3:0.2] Multidimensional poverty | Deprivation in health, education, living standards | National MPI (NITI Aayog)
[123:3:1] - India's official poverty line is **consumption-based (MPCE)**, not income-based.
[123:3:2] - **MPCE 2011-12 (NSS 68th round, MMRP):** about **₹1,430 rural** and **₹2,630 urban** – a gap of about **₹1,200** (urban ~84% higher).
[123:3:3] - **Causes (NextGen):** **illiteracy and lack of quality education** (main cause for rural and tribal poor), unemployment, disguised unemployment in agriculture, discrimination, health costs, inequality.
[123:3:4] - **Social indicators:** illiteracy, malnutrition, poor health care, lack of safe drinking water and sanitation; **size of the house is NOT** one.
[123:3:5] - **Culture of poverty:** **Oscar Lewis (1959)** – fatalism and poverty passed down generations.
[123:3:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society G2 Part 1 p.65-66; web: MoSPI NSS 68th round key indicators (corporatelawreporter.com); app notes 2:123 sub 0
## SUB 4 | Poverty Estimation – Expert Groups
[123:4:0] TABLE head: Committee | Set up / Report | Method | Line / estimate
  [123:4:0.0] Dandekar & Rath | 1971 | First poverty-line study; 2,250 calories | –
  [123:4:0.1] Y.K. Alagh Task Force | 1979 | Calories only: 2,400 rural, 2,100 urban | Spending to buy those calories
  [123:4:0.2] Lakdawala Expert Group | Set up 1989, report 1993 | State-specific lines; CPI-AL (rural), CPI-IW (urban) | 2004-05: 27.5%
  [123:4:0.3] Tendulkar Expert Group | Set up 2005, report 2009 | Dropped calorie anchor; MRP; urban basket for both; health and education included | 2004-05: 37.2%; 2011-12: 21.9%
  [123:4:0.4] S.R. Hashim Expert Group | 2009 | Identifying urban BPL households | –
  [123:4:0.5] N.C. Saxena Expert Group | 2009 | Method of the rural BPL census | –
  [123:4:0.6] C. Rangarajan Expert Group | Set up 2012, report 2014 | Food + non-food (housing, clothing, education, health, transport) | 2011-12: ₹32/day rural, ₹47/day urban (₹972 / ₹1,407 a month)
[123:4:1] - **Latest:** **RBI (Oct 2025)** updated the Rangarajan line with **HCES 2022-23**; **Economic Survey 2025-26:** Tendulkar-line poverty **21.9% (2011-12) → 2.3% (2023-24)**.
[123:4:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 04 p.24; Rocket Indian Economy p.4, p.51; app notes 2:123 sub 1
## SUB 5 | Measurement – Agencies, Surveys and the National MPI
[123:5:0] TABLE head: Body / survey | Role
  [123:5:0.0] NITI Aayog (earlier Planning Commission) | Nodal agency for poverty estimation; uses NSSO data
  [123:5:0.1] NSSO (now NSO, MoSPI) | HCES about every 5 years; MPCE sets the line
  [123:5:0.2] PLFS (NSO) | The standard for unemployment data
  [123:5:0.3] National MPI | NITI Aayog + UNDP + OPHI
[123:5:1] - **PLFS status:** usual status = reference **year**; **CWS = 7 days**; **CDS** = each day of the reference week.
[123:5:2] - **National MPI:** **3 equally weighted dimensions** (health, education, standard of living), **12 indicators**; standard-of-living indicators: cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, housing, electricity, assets, **bank accounts** (nutrition is a **health** indicator).
[123:5:3] TABLE head: NITI MPI 2023 (2019-21 data) | Figure
  [123:5:3.0] India headcount | 14.96%
  [123:5:3.1] Highest | Bihar (33.76%)
  [123:5:3.2] Lowest | Kerala
  [123:5:3.3] Andhra Pradesh | 6.06%; ranked 9th
[123:5:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 04 p.24; app notes 2:123 sub 2-3
## SUB 6 | Unemployment – Types and Data
[123:6:0] TABLE head: Type | Meaning | Predominant area
  [123:6:0.0] Disguised | More workers than needed; extra workers add near-zero output | Agriculture (family farms)
  [123:6:0.1] Seasonal | Work only in some months | Agriculture
  [123:6:0.2] Structural | Mismatch between skills and jobs | Whole economy
  [123:6:0.3] Cyclical | Fall in labour demand in a slowdown | Industry and services
  [123:6:0.4] Frictional | Temporary, while changing or searching for jobs | Urban labour market
  [123:6:0.5] Educated | Joblessness among the educated | Urban areas
[123:6:1] - Disguised and seasonal = rural/agriculture; educated and frictional = urban.
[123:6:2] # Unemployment data (PLFS)
[123:6:3] TABLE head: Indicator | Figure
  [123:6:3.0] India unemployment rate | 6.1% (PLFS 2017-18, a "45-year high") → 3.2% (2023-24)
  [123:6:3.1] AP unemployment rate | 4.1% (PLFS 2023-24)
  [123:6:3.2] AP LFPR | 47.5% (PLFS 2023-24)
[123:6:4] ~~ Sources: web: business-standard.com 31 May 2019 (PLFS 6.1%); app notes 2:123 sub 4
## SUB 7 | Poverty by Social Group; Informal Labour
[123:7:0] - **Scheduled Tribes** have the **highest poverty**, followed by **Scheduled Castes** (ST > SC > others); cause: **discrimination and social exclusion**, landlessness, remoteness.
[123:7:1] - Poverty, unemployment and exclusion **reinforce each other**; responses: MGNREGA/VB-G RAM G, SHG self-employment (SGSY, DAY-NRLM), protective measures for SCs/STs.
[123:7:2] TABLE head: Indicator (2025-26) | Figure
  [123:7:2.0] AP rural informal employment | 62.3%
  [123:7:2.1] Gig workers | 2%+ of the workforce
  [123:7:2.2] Social protection coverage | 22% (2016) → 64.3% (2025)
[123:7:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society G2 Part 1 p.65; app notes 2:123 sub 8-9

=== NOTES 2:124 | Human Rights – Concept, Generations, Udhr, Iccpr, Icescr and Un Machinery
## SUB 0 | Concept of Human Rights – Meaning, Thinkers and Milestones
[124:0:0] # Meaning
[124:0:1] - **Human rights:** rights given to **all human beings by nature**, simply because they are human – **inherent, inalienable, universal**; essential conditions of social life without which no one can lead a normal life.
[124:0:2] - **Core value:** **dignity of man as a human being** (UDHR Preamble: inherent dignity and equal rights); **indivisible and interdependent** – civil-political and socio-economic rights stand together (**Vienna Declaration, 1993**).
[124:0:3] - **Rights vs the State:** rights are **claims of the citizens against the State** – limits on State power, not claims of the State on citizens or privileges of a few.
[124:0:4] - Every **Fundamental Right** is a human right, but **not every human right is a Fundamental Right**.
[124:0:5] - **Kinds of rights:** **economic rights** give a **reasonable and legal source of livelihood** (work, wages, leisure); **political rights** = vote, contest, hold office (the **right to vote is a political right**; in India only a **statutory right** – **Sec. 62, RP Act 1951**, not an FR); civil rights = life, liberty, religion.
[124:0:6] - **Values:** "respect for human rights and responsibilities" is a **constitutional value**; in a **democracy** equality is accepted as a **legal norm**, which makes it easier to guarantee women's freedom and dignity (it does not ensure equal representation).
[124:0:7] - **Violations (NDA 2010):** detaining a person on the way to vote and killing a civilian in a combing operation are **both** human-rights violations.
[124:0:8] # Thinkers
[124:0:9] TABLE head: Thinker | Idea
  [124:0:9.0] John Locke (English/British thinker) | Natural rights – life, liberty, property; popularised the doctrine; "father" of the human-rights idea
  [124:0:9.1] J.J. Rousseau | "Man is born free, but everywhere he is in chains" (Social Contract, 1762)
  [124:0:9.2] Ronald Dworkin (printed "Ronald Darwin") | Rights as trumps: a protective shield for the individual when the State interferes with civil liberties
  [124:0:9.3] Jack Donnelly (printed "John Dowski") | Human rights as a new standard of civilisation (1998)
  [124:0:9.4] Olympe de Gouges | Declaration of the Rights of Woman and the Female Citizen (1791), French Revolution
  [124:0:9.5] Mary Wollstonecraft | A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) – not the 1791 Declaration
[124:0:10] # Milestones
[124:0:11] TABLE head: Year | Document
  [124:0:11.0] 1215 | Magna Carta – charter of liberties signed by the English King (John); first document of the human-rights campaign
  [124:0:11.1] 1688 | Glorious Revolution (Bill of Rights 1689), England
  [124:0:11.2] 1776 | US Declaration of Independence
  [124:0:11.3] 1789 | French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
  [124:0:11.4] 1948 | UDHR
[124:0:12] - **India:** **Indian Civil Liberties Union** founded **24 Aug 1936** (Jawaharlal Nehru and others); **Bhargava Commission (AP, 1977)** on civil-liberties demands.
[124:0:13] > Asked as "who said / who propounded": Locke (natural rights) 3 times; Rousseau's chains line; garbled names (Darwin = Dworkin, Dowski = Donnelly).

## SUB 1 | UDHR 1948 and Human Rights Day
[124:1:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [124:1:0.0] Adopted by | UN General Assembly, 10 December 1948 (Paris)
  [124:1:0.1] Human Rights Day | 10 December every year (UNGA resolution 423(V), 1950)
  [124:1:0.2] Drafting chair | Eleanor Roosevelt
  [124:1:0.3] Structure | Preamble + 30 articles
  [124:1:0.4] Legal status | A declaration – not a treaty, not legally binding
  [124:1:0.5] Core value | Human dignity
[124:1:1] - **Covers** civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights; **guides the SDGs Agenda** (not the Paris Agreement, Magna Carta or NAFTA).
[124:1:2] - **Included:** dignity, liberty, equality (Art. 1); **life, liberty, security (Art. 3)**; equality before law (Art. 7); **privacy (Art. 12)**; social security (Art. 22); **work (Art. 23)**; **adequate standard of living (Art. 25)**; **education (Art. 26)**; **duties to the community (Art. 29)**.
[124:1:3] - **Art. 25(1):** security in the event of **unemployment, sickness, disability, widowhood, old age** – linked to an adequate standard of living (food, clothing, housing, medical care).
[124:1:4] - **NOT included:** **right to universal basic income** (JPSC 2023).
[124:1:5] - **⚠ Privacy IS a UDHR right (Art. 12)** and an ICCPR right (Art. 17); the JPSC 2016 key that called privacy "not a UN-listed human right" is wrong.
[124:1:6] - **Context dates:** UN Day **24 Oct 1945**; India's Constitution adopted 26 Nov 1949.
[124:1:7] # Days and themes
[124:1:8] TABLE head: Day | Date
  [124:1:8.0] Human Rights Day | 10 December
  [124:1:8.1] Universal (International) Children's Day | 20 November (UNCRC adopted 20 Nov 1989)
  [124:1:8.2] UN Day | 24 October
  [124:1:8.3] World Health Day | 7 April
  [124:1:8.4] Labour Day | 1 May
[124:1:9] # Human Rights Day themes
[124:1:10] TABLE head: Year | Human Rights Day theme
  [124:1:10.0] 2016 | "Stand up for someone's rights today"
  [124:1:10.1] 2024 | "Our Rights, Our Future, Right Now"
  [124:1:10.2] 2025 | "Human Rights, Our Everyday Essentials"
[124:1:11] > 10 December asked five times; 2016 theme three times (APPSC Group 2 Mains 2017).
[124:1:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society G2 Part 3 p.42-43; Rocket Indian Society p.68; web: un.org UDHR text (Arts. 12, 25, 26, 29, fetched); app notes 2:124 sub 2
## SUB 2 | Generations of Human Rights
[124:2:0] - **Karel Vasak (1977)** classified rights into three generations, linked to **liberty, equality, fraternity**.
[124:2:1] TABLE head: Generation | Ideal | Rights
  [124:2:1.0] First | Liberty | Civil and political: life, speech, fair trial, vote, participation in political life
  [124:2:1.1] Second | Equality | Economic, social, cultural: work, education, health, social security, eradication of social discrimination
  [124:2:1.2] Third | Fraternity / solidarity | Collective: healthy environment, development, peace
[124:2:2] - **Right to Education** and **Right to Work** are both **second-generation** (ICESCR) rights; Liberty and Equality before law are first-generation.
[124:2:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 2:124 sub 1; general knowledge, not checked (Vasak 1977)
## SUB 3 | International Bill of Human Rights and Core Treaties
[124:3:0] - **International Bill of Human Rights = UDHR + ICCPR + ICESCR + optional protocols.**
[124:3:1] TABLE head: Instrument | Adopted | In force | Key content
  [124:3:1.0] ICESCR | 16 Dec 1966 | 3 Jan 1976 | Work, social security, health, education; realised progressively
  [124:3:1.1] ICCPR | 16 Dec 1966 | 23 Mar 1976 | Life (Art. 6), no torture (Art. 7), fair trial (Art. 14), privacy (Art. 17), expression (Art. 19), child rights (Art. 24)
  [124:3:1.2] ICCPR First Optional Protocol | 1966 | – | Individual complaints
  [124:3:1.3] ICESCR Optional Protocol | 2008 | – | Complaints
[124:3:2] - **ICESCR entered into force first** (Jan 1976), ICCPR in March 1976.
[124:3:3] - **India** acceded to both Covenants on **10 April 1979**; has **not signed the ICCPR First Optional Protocol**.
[124:3:4] - **Child rights:** **ICCPR Art. 24** (also Art. 24 of the Indian Constitution – child labour).
[124:3:5] TABLE head: Treaty | Subject | India
  [124:3:5.0] CERD (1965) | Racial discrimination | Ratified 1968
  [124:3:5.1] CEDAW (1979) | Discrimination against women | Ratified 1993
  [124:3:5.2] CAT (1984) | Torture | Signed 1997, not ratified
  [124:3:5.3] CRC (1989) | Child rights | Acceded 11 Dec 1992
  [124:3:5.4] CMW (1990) | Migrant workers | Not signed
  [124:3:5.5] CRPD (2006) | Persons with disabilities | Ratified 2007 → RPwD Act 2016 (disabilities 7 → 21)
  [124:3:5.6] CPED (2006) | Enforced disappearance | Signed 2007, not ratified
[124:3:6] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Part 2 p.230 (footnote: Covenants, India acceded 10 Apr 1979); app notes 2:124 sub 3-4
## SUB 4 | UN Machinery – Human Rights Council, OHCHR, Paris Principles
[124:4:0] # Human Rights Council (UNHRC)
[124:4:1] - Set up **2006**, replacing the **UN Commission on Human Rights**; based in **Geneva**.
[124:4:2] - **47 members** elected by the UNGA; **3-year terms**, at most **two consecutive** terms; **two-thirds** UNGA vote can suspend a member.
[124:4:3] TABLE head: Region | Seats
  [124:4:3.0] Africa | 13
  [124:4:3.1] Asia-Pacific | 13
  [124:4:3.2] Latin America and Caribbean | 8
  [124:4:3.3] Western Europe and Others | 7
  [124:4:3.4] Eastern Europe | 6
[124:4:4] - **Universal Periodic Review (UPR):** peer review of every UN member's record; since **2008**, cycles of about **4.5 years**.
[124:4:5] - **Special rapporteurs** ("special procedures") = **unpaid independent experts**; **treaty bodies** monitor each core treaty.
[124:4:6] - **OHCHR** set up **1993**, after the **Vienna Conference**.
[124:4:7] # Paris Principles and NHRIs
[124:4:8] - Adopted by the **UNGA in 1993** (drafted in Paris, Oct 1991): **independence and autonomy**, **pluralist** composition, adequate resources, **powers to investigate** (not dependence on the executive).
[124:4:9] - **GANHRI** accredits NHRIs through its **Sub-Committee on Accreditation**: **"A" = fully**, "B" = partly compliant.
[124:4:10] - India's **NHRC** (1993, under the PHRA 1993) is a **statutory** NHRI.
[124:4:11] # Rights newly recognised by the UNGA
[124:4:12] TABLE head: Right | Recognition
  [124:4:12.0] Right to development | Declaration, 1986
  [124:4:12.1] Right to water and sanitation | 28 July 2010
  [124:4:12.2] Right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment | 28 July 2022 – a universal human right
[124:4:13] ~~ Sources: app notes 2:124 sub 5-7; general knowledge, not checked (HRC seats)
## SUB 5 | NGOs and Human Rights Prizes
[124:5:0] TABLE head: Body / award | Facts
  [124:5:0.0] Amnesty International | Global human rights movement (NGO, not a UN body); founded 1961, London, by British lawyer Peter Benenson; 7 million+ people in 150+ countries; Nobel Peace Prize 1977
  [124:5:0.1] Human Rights Watch | New York-based NGO
  [124:5:0.2] UN Human Rights Prize | Given by the UNGA, usually every five years, since 1968
[124:5:1] - **Amnesty is NOT a UN organ** (UN principal organs include the General Assembly, ICJ, Trusteeship Council) and not part of the **National Disaster Management Plan for animals** (NIDM, World Animal Protection, Policy Perspectives Foundation are).
[124:5:2] - **Match (UPSC 2008):** Amnesty – Peter Benenson; CIS – **Viskuli**; Danube Commission – **Belgrade Convention**; European Space Agency – **Paris**.
[124:5:3] - **UN Human Rights Prize 2018:** **Rebeca Gyumi** (Tanzania, rights of **women and girls**), **Asma Jahangir** (Pakistan, posthumous), **Joênia Wapichana** (Brazil, indigenous rights), **Front Line Defenders** (Ireland).

[n09d2fefb620] sub0
  In India, what kind of right is the right to vote?
  Fundamental Right under Article 19 | *Statutory right under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act | Directive Principle under Article 47 | Fundamental Duty under Article 51A
  x: The right to vote is only a statutory right, conferred by Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act. It is not a Fundamental Right (Art. 19 lists freedoms of speech, movement etc.), a Directive Principle (Art. 47 concerns nutrition, health and prohibition) or a Fundamental Duty. This shows that not every human right is a Fundamental Right.

=== NOTES 2:128 | Women's Rights – Constitutional Provisions and the Legal Framework
## SUB 0 | Reform Laws of the Colonial Era and the Reformers
[128:0:0] TABLE head: Law | Year | Reformer / note
  [128:0:0.0] Bengal Sati Regulation | 1829 | Banned sati in British India; campaign of Raja Rammohan Roy; Lord William Bentinck
  [128:0:0.1] Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act | 1856 | Due to Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar; children of such marriages legitimate
  [128:0:0.2] Female Infanticide Prevention Act | 1870 | Colonial law (APPSC 2018)
  [128:0:0.3] Child Marriage Restraint (Sarda) Act | 1929 | Replaced by the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006
  [128:0:0.4] Hindu Marriage Act | 1955 | After Independence
[128:0:1] - **Order:** Sati 1829 → Widow Remarriage 1856 → Sarda 1929 → Hindu Marriage Act 1955.
[128:0:2] - **⚠ Trap:** widow remarriage = **1856** (not 1855, 1879, 1893) – asked ×4; an exam of 2000 asking the "Prohibition of Child Marriage Act" meant the **1929** Sarda Act.
[128:0:3] TABLE head: Reformer | Reform
  [128:0:3.0] Raja Rammohan Roy | Abolition of sati (1829); Brahmo Samaj (1828); *Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin*; *Sambad Kaumudi*
  [128:0:3.1] Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar | Widow Remarriage Act 1856; Bethune School (1849); against child marriage, polygamy
  [128:0:3.2] Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule | First girls' school, Pune, 1848; Satyashodhak Samaj (1873, Jyotirao); infanticide home 1863; *Gulamgiri*
  [128:0:3.3] Savitribai Phule | India's first woman teacher
  [128:0:3.4] Pandita Ramabai | Arya Mahila Samaj (1882); *The High-Caste Hindu Woman* (1887)
  [128:0:3.5] Tarabai Shinde | *Stri Purush Tulana*
  [128:0:3.6] Kandukuri Veeresalingam | First Telugu widow remarriage, Rajahmundry, 1881
[128:0:4] - *The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna* = **Mahendranath Gupta ('M')**.
[128:0:5] # Status of Women Through History
[128:0:6] - **Vedic:** wife honoured as **'Ardhangini'** (better half). **Later Vedic and medieval:** decline; **purdah** prominent.
[128:0:7] TABLE head: Custom | Meaning / law
  [128:0:7.0] Niyoga | Childless widow/wife has a son by the husband's brother or kinsman (not a ban on widow remarriage)
  [128:0:7.1] Devadasi | Girls dedicated to temples; banned in AP by both the Madras Act 1947 and the AP Devadasis (Prohibition of Dedication) Act 1988
[128:0:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Society p.1 l.18-27, p.39 l.1724-1725, p.99 (PCMA replaced Sarda Act); Spectrum Modern India l.9267-9270; app notes 2:128 sub 0-1
## SUB 1 | Laws on Women – Chronology
[128:1:0] TABLE head: Act | Year | Key point
  [128:1:0.0] Indian Succession Act | 1925 | Christians and others (not Muslims)
  [128:1:0.1] Special Marriage Act | 1954 | Civil, secular marriage
  [128:1:0.2] Hindu Succession Act | 1956 | Property rights
  [128:1:0.3] Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act | 1956 | Trafficking for prostitution
  [128:1:0.4] Dowry Prohibition Act | 1961 (not 1976) | Bans giving, taking, demanding dowry
  [128:1:0.5] Maternity Benefit Act | 1961 | Maternity protection
  [128:1:0.6] MTP Act | 1971 | Abortion law
  [128:1:0.7] Equal Remuneration Act | 1976 | Equal pay; prevents gender-based pay discrimination
  [128:1:0.8] Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act | 1986 | Ads, publications, paintings (not child marriage)
  [128:1:0.9] Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act | 1987 | Sati and its glorification
  [128:1:0.10] PCPNDT Act | 1994; in force 1 Jan 1996 | Bans prenatal sex determination
  [128:1:0.11] Domestic Violence Act | 2005 | Civil remedy; Right to Residence (s.17)
  [128:1:0.12] Prohibition of Child Marriage Act | 2006 | Replaced Sarda Act; 18 F / 21 M
  [128:1:0.13] POSH Act | 2013 | Internal Committee at 10+ employees
  [128:1:0.14] Criminal Law (Amendment) Act | 2013 | After Nirbhaya
[128:1:1] - **Match (TSPSC 2023):** Equal Remuneration **1976**, Sati **1987**, Indian Succession **1925**, Dowry **1961**.
[128:1:2] - **Telangana/AP women's laws in order:** PCPNDT **1994** → AP Compulsory Registration of Marriages **2002** → Prohibition of Child Marriage **2006** → POSH **2013**.
[128:1:3] - **Constitutional vs legal rights:** the ban on dowry is a **legal** right (1961 Act), not a constitutional one.
[128:1:4] - **Marital rape exception (BNS s.63)** under challenge in SC (10 Sep 2026).
[128:1:5] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Society p.39-41 l.1724-1817, p.99; NextGen Society Part 3 p.35; app notes 2:128 sub 6
## SUB 2 | Personal Laws, Succession and Adoption
[128:2:0] TABLE head: Law | Provision
  [128:2:0.0] Special Marriage Act 1954 | Civil, secular marriage irrespective of religion, after public notice
  [128:2:0.1] Hindu Marriage Act 1955 | Monogamy, divorce grounds, restitution of conjugal rights
  [128:2:0.2] Hindu Succession Act 1956 | Equal inheritance; ended female heir's limited estate; covers patrilineal (Mitakshara, Dayabhaga) and matrilineal (Marumakkattayam, Aliyasantana) systems (s.7, s.17); s.2(2) excludes notified STs
  [128:2:0.3] HSA (Amendment) 2005 | Daughters = equal coparceners
  [128:2:0.4] AP HSA Amendment | 1985 under NTR: unmarried daughters coparceners, before 2005
  [128:2:0.5] Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act 1956 | Male adopting a girl must be at least 21 years older (s.11)
  [128:2:0.6] Muslim Women (Divorce) Act 1986 | After Shah Bano
  [128:2:0.7] Muslim Women (Marriage) Act 2019 | Instant talaq-e-biddat void and illegal; up to 3 years
[128:2:1] - **HSA disqualification:** **conversion** (convert's descendants, s.26), murder (s.25); **no** disqualification for disease, defect or deformity (s.28).
[128:2:2] - **⚠ Trap:** the 1929 Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act only reordered heirs under Mitakshara – the law that brought both matrilineal and patrilineal Hindus under one code is the **HSA 1956**.
[128:2:3] - **Art. 44 (UCC)** rests on the idea that **religion and personal law are different** in a civilised society (Sarla Mudgal 1995).
[128:2:4] - Maintenance: **Sec. 125 CrPC → Sec. 144 BNSS**. **SC (8 Oct 2025):** upheld HSA exclusion of STs.
[128:2:5] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Society p.41, p.99; web: courtbook.in HSA s.17; general knowledge (HAMA s.11, HSA s.25-28); app notes 2:128 sub 7
## SUB 3 | Constitutional Provisions

  [128:3:0.7] 330A / 332A | 1/3 seats in Lok Sabha / State Assemblies
[128:3:1] - All of 14, 15, 15(3), 39, 42, 51A(e) are women's safeguards (APPSC Panchayat Secretary).
[128:3:2] - **⚠ Trap:** maternity relief = **Art. 42**, not 39(f), 47 or 51A(e).
[128:3:3] # 106th Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023)

[128:3:8] - **AP:** **50%** in panchayats and municipalities; **50% of nominated posts** and work contracts (14 Apr 2026); **33 1/3% horizontal** reservation in direct recruitment.

## SUB 8 | Gender Concepts, Indices and Thinkers
[128:8:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [128:8:0.0] Patriarchy | Men hold primary power and status
  [128:8:0.1] Gender discrimination | Unequal treatment of men and women by society
  [128:8:0.2] Gender mainstreaming | Gender perspective in all policies, laws, institutions (Beijing 1995); aims: reduce discrimination, equitable development, inclusive governance
  [128:8:0.3] Gender audit | Check of policies, programmes, institutions and budgets: gender budgeting, equal opportunity, workplace safety, decision-making
  [128:8:0.4] GDI | Female-to-male ratio: health, education, command over resources
  [128:8:0.5] GII | 0 (equality) to 1 (worst)
  [128:8:0.6] Global Gender Gap (WEF) | Economy, education, health, politics (not military spending)
[128:8:1] - **Global Gender Gap 2025:** India **131st of 148**. Women, Peace and Security Index 2023: **131/177**.
[128:8:2] - Sex ratio NFHS-4 **991** → NFHS-5 **1020**; SRB **904 → 917** (2021-23). Most male-skewed: **Haryana, Punjab**. Causes: son preference, foeticide, dowry (not equal inheritance or schooling). Women's LFPR **37%** (2022-23).
[128:8:3] - **Drought:** **women** suffer most (water, fuel, food, wages).

## SUB 9 | Reproductive Rights – MTP, Surrogacy, ART, PCPNDT
[128:9:0] TABLE head: Law | Permitted | Prohibited / limit
  [128:9:0.0] MTP 1971 (in force 1 Apr 1972); Amendment 2021 | 24 weeks for special categories | Disclosing the woman's identity
  [128:9:0.1] Surrogacy (Regulation) Act 2021 (Bill 2019) | Altruistic only; essentiality and eligibility certificates; close relative as surrogate | Commercial surrogacy; surrogate only once
  [128:9:0.2] ART (Regulation) Act 2021 | Registered clinics/banks | Sex-selective ART; sale of gametes
  [128:9:0.3] PCPNDT 1994 | Tests for genetic abnormality | Sex determination

=== NOTES 2:129 | Laws for Women – Dowry, Domestic Violence, Posh, Maternity Benefit and Trafficking
## SUB 0 | Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961
[129:0:0] - **Enacted 1961; in force 1 July 1961** (not 1955, 1976, 20 May or 1 June). The **1st joint sitting** of Parliament was on the Dowry Prohibition Bill.
[129:0:1] - **Section 2 – Dowry:** **any property or valuable security** given or agreed to be given, **directly or indirectly**, before, at or any time after marriage, in connection with the marriage.
[129:0:2] - **Not dowry:** **dower/mahr** (Muslim personal law); **presents given without demand and entered in a list** under the rules (s.3(2)).
[129:0:3] TABLE head: Section | Provision
  [129:0:3.0] s.3 | Giving/taking/abetting: not less than 5 years + fine ≥ ₹15,000 or dowry value, whichever is more
  [129:0:3.1] s.4 | Demanding dowry: 6 months to 2 years + fine up to ₹10,000
  [129:0:3.2] s.8A | Burden of proof on the accused
  [129:0:3.3] s.8B | Dowry Prohibition Officers appointed by the State Government
[129:0:4] - Offences are **cognisable, non-bailable and non-compoundable**.
[129:0:5] - **1986 amendment** brought **dowry death** (IPC 304B, now BNS 80) and its presumption (Evidence Act 113B, now BSA 118); also amended 1984.
[129:0:6] - **⚠ Trap:** 5 years is the **minimum**; any payment **on demand** (to the groom's father, sister …) is dowry.
[129:0:7] - Weak enforcement: **poor enforcement, faulty FIRs**, deaths shown as accidents/suicides; about **20 dowry deaths a day**; **UP, Bihar, MP, Rajasthan** lead.
[129:0:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Society p.39, p.99 l.4630; app notes 2:129 sub 1
## SUB 1 | Sexual Harassment at Workplace – Vishaka and POSH Act 2013
[129:1:0] - **Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997):** SC guidelines against sexual harassment of **working women at the workplace** (Arts 14, 19, 21) → **POSH Act, 2013** evolved from the **Vishaka guidelines** (asked ×4).
[129:1:1] - Full name: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (**Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal**) Act, 2013; **in force 9 December 2013**.
[129:1:2] TABLE head: Committee | Where | Composition
  [129:1:2.0] Internal Committee (IC) | Every workplace with 10 or more employees | Senior woman employee as Presiding Officer; 2+ employees; 1 NGO member; half women
  [129:1:2.1] Local Committee (LC) | District; constituted by the District Officer | Workplaces with fewer than 10, or complaint against the employer
[129:1:3] - **Time limits:**
[129:1:4] TABLE head: Step | Time limit
  [129:1:4.0] Complaint | Within 3 months (extendable by 3)
  [129:1:4.1] Inquiry | Within 90 days
  [129:1:4.2] Employer action | Within 60 days
[129:1:5] - Harassment includes **showing pornography**, unwelcome contact, demands for sexual favours.
[129:1:6] - **SHe-Box:** online complaint system for workplace sexual harassment, **single window for every woman** whatever her work status – organised or unorganised, private or public; **SHe-Box 2.0** (Mission Shakti) also tracks ICs/LCs.
[129:1:7] - **AP:** **26 LCs**, **10,437 ICs** (AP SES 2025-26).
[129:1:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Society p.88, p.96 l.4464, p.99; NextGen Society Part 1 p.77-78; app notes 2:129 sub 3
## SUB 2 | Domestic Violence Act 2005 and Section 498A
[129:2:0] - **Enacted 2005; in force 26 October 2006**; a **civil law**.
[129:2:1] - **Section 3:** physical, sexual, **verbal/emotional** and **economic** abuse.
[129:2:2] - **Protection Officers** appointed by the **State Government**; relief by **Magistrate**. **AP:** Protection Officers = **DWCDA Project Directors and RDOs**.
[129:2:3] TABLE head: Relief | Section
  [129:2:3.0] Right to reside | 17
  [129:2:3.1] Protection order | 18
  [129:2:3.2] Residence order | 19
  [129:2:3.3] Monetary relief | 20
  [129:2:3.4] Custody / compensation | 21 / 22
[129:2:4] - **Why domestic violence is common:** social acceptance of wife torture, violence in society reflected in the family, emotional instability – a victim's **tolerating** it is a response, not a cause (CSP 1996).
[129:2:5] - **Rajesh Sharma v. State of UP (2017):** Family Welfare Committees in every district; 498A complaints referred to them; no routine arrest before their report; NRIs also covered (no routine passport impounding).
[129:2:6] - **⚠ Outdated:** FWC directions **withdrawn** in **Social Action Forum v. UoI (14 Sep 2018)**; 498A is now **BNS 85-86**.
[129:2:7] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Society p.88, p.99 l.4651; app notes 2:129 sub 2; sci.gov.in (via app explanation)
## SUB 3 | Other Acts – Sati, Indecent Representation, ITPA and Dates in Force
[129:3:0] TABLE head: Law | Enacted | In force / note
  [129:3:0.0] Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act | 1956 (as SITA) | Amended 1978; renamed ITPA by the 1986 amendment

## SUB 5 | Trafficking – Constitution, Laws and Reports
[129:5:0] - **Article 23** prohibits **traffic in human beings, begar** and forced labour; **Article 24** bars children below 14 in factories, mines, hazardous work.
[129:5:1] - **ITPA 1956** primarily addresses **trafficked women** (commercial sexual exploitation); does **not** punish prostitution itself – punishes **brothel-keeping, soliciting, living on earnings**.
[129:5:2] - **CLA 2013** definition covers all forms **irrespective of consent** (sex trafficking, forced labour, slavery, organ removal).
[129:5:3] - **UNODC:** high origin – Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Pakistan; high destination – **India and Pakistan**.
[129:5:4] - **US TIP Report:** **Tier 1** = only tier fully meeting minimum standards; Tier 2, Tier 2 Watch List, Tier 3.
[129:5:5] - **Anuradha Koirala** (Maiti Nepal): **Padma Shri 2017** for rescuing thousands of **sex-trafficking victims**.
[129:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society Part 3 p.37; Laxmikanth Part 1 l.7645; app notes 2:129 sub 7
